title: Recruiting and Releasing Volunteers
subtitle: The whole church is the ministry, and the pastor's job is to equip the saints for the work, not to do the work while the saints applaud.

sections.title: The One Verse We Get Backward
sections.body:
Ephesians four says God gave pastors and teachers to equip the saints for the work of ministry. Read it slowly, because the church has been reading it backward for a long time.

The work of ministry is the saints' work. The pastor's work is to equip them for it. The minister is not the one who does the ministry while the people watch. The minister is the one who trains the people to do the ministry, so that the body builds itself up in love, every part working. We have inverted this completely. We have built churches where one paid professional does the ministry and the congregation consumes it, and then we wonder why the people are passive and the pastor is exhausted.

Not a minister and an audience. A body, every part working. That is the design, and the pastor who insists on doing it all has not only worn himself out, he has robbed the church of its own calling, because every task he keeps for himself is a task some member was made to do and is now denied. The goal is not a busy pastor and a watching church. The goal is a church at work and a pastor who equipped it.

sections.title: Enlisting Without Begging or Manipulating
sections.body:
Most volunteer recruitment is either begging or guilt, and both produce the wrong workers. The desperate plea from the front, the same eight people doing everything, the guilt trip that fills the slot with someone who resents being there. None of it reflects the dignity of the calling we are inviting people into.

Recruit by vision and by person, not by need. Do not say we are desperate, the nursery is empty, please someone. Say I have watched you with children and I think God made you for this, would you pray about it. The first is a plea for a body to fill a hole. The second is a calling spoken into a particular person, and it is the second that produces a worker who stays, because they are not filling a slot, they are answering a summons.

And recruit personally, face to face, by name. The announcement from the platform recruits no one worth recruiting. The conversation over coffee, where you tell a specific person what you see in them and what God might be inviting them to, recruits the people who become the backbone of the church. It is slower. It is the only way that works. Jesus did not announce for volunteers. He looked at men and said follow me, and called them by name.

sections.title: Equipping People to Actually Succeed
sections.body:
We recruit people and then abandon them, and we are surprised when they quit. The volunteer thrown into a role with no training, no support, and no clear picture of success is a volunteer set up to fail, and their failure is on us, not them.

Equip them. Show them how, do not just tell them. Do the task with them before you ask them to do it alone, the way Jesus took the disciples along before he sent them out. Give them what they need to win, the resources, the training, the clarity about what the role actually is and what success looks like in it. A person equipped to succeed will serve for years. A person dropped into a role to sink will serve for weeks and leave wounded.

And then, the hard part, actually release them. Let them do it their way, not yours. Let them make mistakes you would not have made. The control freak recruits help and then refuses to release control, hovering, correcting, redoing the work the moment the volunteer's back is turned, and there is no faster way to drive away a willing servant than to make them feel they can never do it right. To equip and not release is to recruit your own frustration. Release means the thing gets done differently than you would do it, and you let it, because a kingdom built only the pastor's way is a small kingdom.

sections.title: Equipping People Without Using Them Up
sections.body:
Here is the sin that hides inside even healthy volunteer ministry. We can release people into the work and then consume them, treating willing servants as a resource to be spent rather than souls to be shepherded, until the most committed members are the most burned out and the most likely to leave.

Watch your best people, because they are the ones at risk. They say yes to everything, so we ask them everything, and we pile the load on the faithful precisely because they are faithful, until the faithful break. The cruelest thing a church can do is reward willingness with exhaustion, and we do it constantly, to our most devoted members, and call it their gift in operation.

So protect your volunteers from yourself and from the church. Help them say no. Give roles an end date so service is not a life sentence. Notice when someone is doing too much and take something off them before they collapse, do not wait for the resignation letter. And shepherd them as people, ask about their souls and their families, not only their tasks, because the moment a volunteer becomes a function to you rather than a person, you have started using them up, and they will feel it long before they can name it.

sections.title: The Body That Builds Itself
sections.body:
The measure of a pastor is not how much ministry he does. It is how much ministry happens that he does not do. The church where everything runs through one man is a monument to that man and a failure of his calling, however impressive it looks, because it has trained a congregation to watch instead of work.

The church Paul describes builds itself up. Every part works. The body grows because the parts are doing what God made them to do, and the pastor's joy is not to be the one doing it all but to watch the saints he equipped doing the work of ministry without him, some of it better than he ever did it. That requires a death in the pastor, the death of being needed, the death of being the one everyone depends on.

I have not fully died to it. I still like being needed. I still catch myself keeping the task I should give away, because giving it away means I matter a little less, and the self does not want to matter less. That is the work, and it is never finished.

The goal is a church that would keep ministering if you disappeared tomorrow. Build that, and you will have built the thing Ephesians four describes. Refuse to build it, and you will have built a crowd around yourself and called it a church.
